title: Interleaved KV tiling for tensor-pipeline aligned multi-GPU KV cache
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: As model sizes and sequence lengths grow, the KV cache becomes the dominant GPU memory consumer during inference. Existing slab/shard strategies (global slabs or per-GPU contiguous slabs) interact poorly with combined tensor and pipeline parallelism, causing uneven memory pressure, frequent cross-GPU transfers, and stalls during continuous batching.

Goal: Design and validate an interleaved KV tiling scheme that aligns KV storage with tensor-parallel (TP) tensor partitioning and pipeline-parallel (PP) stage boundaries to: reduce peak per-GPU memory, minimize all-to-all communication during KV lookups and updates, and preserve streaming/continuous batching latency SLOs.

Key ideas:
- Tile-level mapping: split KV per layer into small tiles (tile_len tokens x kv_feature_block) and map tiles to GPUs using an interleaved mapping that follows TP dimension slices. This keeps each GPU holding the exact KV shards needed for its local attention matmuls most of the time.
- PP-aware placement: for models using pipeline parallelism, align tile assignments with pipeline stages so that a GPU that executes a stage holds the preceding layers' KV tiles it will need for autoregressive decoding for tokens entering that stage, reducing cross-stage pull operations.
- Contiguous allocation per tile: allocate tiles as contiguous GPU buffers to improve allocation/defrag performance and enable efficient prefetch into the attention kernel.
- Streaming update protocol: local appends to KV are batched at tile granularity; a lightweight ring-exchange (peer-to-peer) is used only when a GPUS needs a remote tile for attention; otherwise local tiles serve the request.
- Reuse and eviction policy: LRU-on-tiles with size-aware eviction to avoid evicting many small KV rows; support a hot-set hint from continuous batching system to pin frequently-accessed prefix tiles.

Design options considered:
1) Fine-grained interleaving (small tiles ~64 tokens): excellent load balance, high metadata overhead, more P2P operations.
2) Coarse-grained tiling (large tiles ~512-1024 tokens): lower metadata overhead, less P2P overhead, but worse memory balance and potential higher eviction churn.
3) Hybrid adaptive tiling: start coarse and split tiles dynamically when memory imbalance or hotspot access patterns are detected.

Trade-offs and rationale: we chose a medium default tile size (256 tokens x 64-feature blocks) with adaptive splitting heuristic. Medium tile size gives good balance between metadata cost and load balance; adaptive split handles edge cases (very long contexts or skewed prefix popularity).

Planned experiments:
- Microbenchmarks: GPT-style 20B model, sequence lengths 2k and 8k, TP=2/4, PP=1/2, batch sizes 8/16 streaming. Metrics: peak GPU memory, per-GPU memory variance, tail latency (p95/p99), throughput (tokens/sec), and number of P2P exchanges per output token.
- Integration tests: continuous batching enabled with prefix caching on a production-like workload (mixed short/long tails) and measure SLO violations over 24h.
- Failure modes: simulate GPU OOM on one host and validate graceful fallback to remote fetch + lightweight backpressure.

Acceptance criteria:
- Reduce 95th percentile peak per-GPU KV memory by >=20% vs current contiguous-slab baseline for TP=2/4 and PP=1/2 on 2k sequences.
- No more than 10% regression in average latency for streaming requests; p99 should remain within current SLOs.
- P2P exchanges per token should be <2 on average for the mixed workload.

Artifacts and links:
- RFC: Confluence - Distributed KV Tiling RFC (internal) - https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Interleaved+KV+Tiling+RFC
- Spike notebook + perf graphs: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/kv-tiling/spike-results
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4218
- Design diagram (stored in Drive): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1KvTilingDesign

Rollout plan:
- Week 0-2: finalize design and complete prototype microbenchmarks (done).
- Week 3: internal opt-in canary for dedicated test clusters (small traffic).
- Week 4-5: expand canary to more clusters, collect telemetry, tune adaptive split heuristics.
- Week 6: enable by default behind runtime flag and monitor for 2 weeks before wide release.

Risks and mitigations:
- Increased metadata/CPU overhead: mitigate by storing tile metadata in compact bitmaps and batching metadata updates.
- Edge-case cross-GPU hotspots causing P2P storms: mitigate using hotset pinning and backpressure to coalesce requests.
- Interaction with other optimizations (quantization, caching): coordinate with kernel team to ensure contiguous tile buffers are compatible with quantized kernels.

Notes: this ticket focuses on the placement and protocol for multi-GPU KV memory. Separate follow-ups will handle kernel-level prefetch and attention operator changes required for zero-copy access to remote tiles.
